key_terms.meaning: The inclined principal tension from bending and shear together; at the neutral axis σ<sub>1</sub> = τ at 45°.
σ<sub>1</sub> = σ/2 + √((σ/2)² + τ²), σ positive in tension; tan 2θ = 2τ/σ gives its angle θ to the axis.

key_terms.term: Shear carried by a cracked beam
key_terms.meaning: V = V<sub>cz</sub> + V<sub>a</sub> + V<sub>d</sub> + V<sub>s</sub>: compression zone, aggregate interlock, dowel action and stirrups.
τ<sub>v</sub> = V<sub>u</sub>/(b d), V<sub>u</sub> in N, b and d in mm.
IS 456 Table 19 (depends on grade and p<sub>t</sub>) and Table 20 (2.8, 3.1, 3.5 N/mm² for M20, M25, M30).
At d from the support face where the reaction compresses the beam end.
V<sub>us</sub> = 0.87 f<sub>y</sub> A<sub>sv</sub> d/s<sub>v</sub> with V<sub>us</sub> = V<sub>u</sub> − τ<sub>c</sub> b d.
V<sub>us</sub> = 0.87 f<sub>y</sub> A<sub>sv</sub> d (sin α + cos α)/s<sub>v</sub>; a single bent-up bar 0.87 f<sub>y</sub> A<sub>sv</sub> sin α; bent-up bars at most half of the shear steel.
A<sub>sv</sub>/(b s<sub>v</sub>) ≥ 0.4/(0.87 f<sub>y</sub>), f<sub>y</sub> not above 415 N/mm².
Least of 0.75 d and 300 mm (vertical); lesser of d and 300 mm (45° inclined).
V<sub>e</sub> = V<sub>u</sub> + 1.6 T<sub>u</sub>/b; τ<sub>ve</sub> = V<sub>e</sub>/(b d) ≤ τ<sub>c,max</sub>.

A<sub>sv</sub> = T<sub>u</sub> s<sub>v</sub>/(b<sub>1</sub> d<sub>1</sub> 0.87 f<sub>y</sub>) + V<sub>u</sub> s<sub>v</sub>/(2.5 d<sub>1</sub> 0.87 f<sub>y</sub>), not less than (τ<sub>ve</sub> − τ<sub>c</sub>) b s<sub>v</sub>/(0.87 f<sub>y</sub>).
Not more than x<sub>1</sub>, (x<sub>1</sub> + y<sub>1</sub>)/4 and 300 mm.
M<sub>t</sub> = T<sub>u</sub> (1 + D/b)/1.7; M<sub>e1</sub> = M<sub>u</sub> + M<sub>t</sub>; M<sub>e2</sub> = M<sub>t</sub> − M<sub>u</sub> when M<sub>t</sub> > M<sub>u</sub>.
Plain bars in tension 1.2, 1.4, 1.5 N/mm² for M20, M25, M30; deformed bars +60 %; compression +25 %.
L<sub>d</sub> = φ σ<sub>s</sub>/(4 τ<sub>bd</sub>), σ<sub>s</sub> = 0.87 f<sub>y</sub>; 40.3φ for Fe415 deformed bars in M25.
L<sub>d</sub> ≤ 1.3 M<sub>1</sub>/V + L<sub>0</sub> at simple supports (1.3 when the reaction confines the bar ends).
4φ for each 45°, at most 16φ; a 90° bend is 8φ.
Flexural tension: greater of L<sub>d</sub> and 30φ; direct tension: 2 L<sub>d</sub> and 30φ; compression: L<sub>d</sub> in compression and 24φ.
Greater of d and 12φ beyond the theoretical cut-off.
Cover to all steel including stirrups: 20, 30, 45, 50, 75 mm for mild to extreme exposure.
s = (b − 2c − 2φ<sub>s</sub> − nφ)/(n − 1) ≥ greater of φ and aggregate size + 5 mm; ≤ 180 mm for Fe415.

takeaways: Shear cracks are diagonal tension cracks. After cracking the beam carries shear through the compression zone, aggregate interlock, dowel action and stirrups.

Check τ<sub>v</sub> = V<sub>u</sub>/(b d) at d from the support face: below τ<sub>c</sub> give minimum stirrups, up to τ<sub>c,max</sub> design stirrups for V<sub>u</sub> − τ<sub>c</sub> b d, above τ<sub>c,max</sub> enlarge the section.
Stirrups follow from V<sub>us</sub> = 0.87 f<sub>y</sub> A<sub>sv</sub> d/s<sub>v</sub>; round the spacing down and respect the minimum steel and the 0.75 d and 300 mm limits.
Equilibrium torsion must be designed; compatibility torsion may be ignored if torsional stiffness is ignored in the analysis.

Torsion needs closed stirrups and longitudinal corner bars: V<sub>e</sub> checks the section, T<sub>u</sub> and V<sub>u</sub> size the stirrups, M<sub>e1</sub> = M<sub>u</sub> + M<sub>t</sub> sizes the bars, and M<sub>e2</sub> appears when M<sub>t</sub> > M<sub>u</sub>.
Development length L<sub>d</sub> = φ σ<sub>s</sub>/(4 τ<sub>bd</sub>) depends only on the bar, the steel and the concrete; use the deformed-bar bond stress for TMT bars.
At simple supports check L<sub>d</sub> ≤ 1.3 M<sub>1</sub>/V + L<sub>0</sub> and run a third of the bars into the support for L<sub>d</sub>/3.
Laps are the greater of L<sub>d</sub> and 30φ in flexural tension, based on the smaller bar, staggered and away from high moment; curtailed bars run d or 12φ past the theoretical cut-off.
Detailing (cover, spacing, hooks, side-face bars and the bar bending schedule) decides whether the calculated steel can actually work.
bank_note: Long answers on shear, torsion and bond want the behaviour and the code procedure together: why the crack forms, then τ<sub>v</sub> against τ<sub>c</sub>; why the space truss needs closed stirrups, then V<sub>e</sub> and M<sub>e1</sub>. Most syllabi set one full design (stirrups, or combined bending, shear and torsion) and one question on bond, anchorage and detailing.

bank.q: Explain how a reinforced concrete beam resists shear before and after diagonal cracking. Name each contribution after cracking and explain the modes of shear failure.
outline: Uncracked: σ and τ combine into principal tension; 45° at the neutral axis
After cracking V = V<sub>cz</sub> + V<sub>a</sub> + V<sub>d</sub> + V<sub>s</sub>
Which mechanisms fade as the crack widens; role of stirrups
answer: Before cracking. At any point the bending stress σ and the shear stress τ = V Q/(I b) combine into a principal tension σ<sub>1</sub> = σ/2 + √((σ/2)² + τ²) at an angle θ with tan 2θ = 2τ/σ. At the soffit τ = 0, so σ<sub>1</sub> is horizontal; at the neutral axis σ = 0, so σ<sub>1</sub> = τ at 45°.

answer.text: Numbers for an uncracked M25 beam 300 × 600 mm with M = 60 kN·m and V = 120 kN:

answer: Cracking. Concrete cracks when σ<sub>1</sub> reaches its tensile strength (about 2 to 3 N/mm² in direct tension for M25). The crack forms at right angles to σ<sub>1</sub>, so it starts vertical at the soffit and bends towards the load: a flexure-shear crack. In thin webs a web-shear crack can open first at the neutral axis near a support.

After cracking the shear is carried by four parts, V = V<sub>cz</sub> + V<sub>a</sub> + V<sub>d</sub> + V<sub>s</sub>: the uncracked compression zone above the crack (V<sub>cz</sub>); aggregate interlock, friction between the rough crack faces (V<sub>a</sub>); dowel action of the main bars crossing the crack (V<sub>d</sub>); and the stirrups crossing the crack (V<sub>s</sub>).

As the crack widens, aggregate interlock falls fastest, and dowel action is lost when the cover under the bars splits. Stirrups hold the crack narrow, so they also keep V<sub>a</sub> and V<sub>d</sub> working. This is why IS 456 requires at least minimum stirrups everywhere.

Truss analogy: compression zone = top chord, tension steel = bottom chord, concrete between cracks = 45° struts, stirrups = vertical ties. It gives V<sub>us</sub> = 0.87 f<sub>y</sub> A<sub>sv</sub> d/s<sub>v</sub>, because a 45° crack crosses d/s<sub>v</sub> stirrups.

Failure modes, by shear span ratio a/d: below about 1, arch action with crushing or splitting of the strut; about 1 to 2.5, shear-compression (crushing above the crack); about 2.5 to 6, diagonal tension (sudden splitting, the most brittle); above about 6, flexure governs. In thin webs the struts can crush (web crushing), which stirrups cannot prevent and which τ<sub>c,max</sub> guards against.

Check: the numbers in the table give σ<sub>1</sub> ≤ 3.5 N/mm² (= 0.7√25) at every point, so that beam is still uncracked; at a larger load the neutral-axis value reaches the tensile strength first, which is why shear cracks are inclined.

bank.q: Define nominal shear stress, design shear strength of concrete and maximum shear stress. Explain the three cases of the IS 456 shear check and why the critical section is at d from the support face.
outline: τ<sub>c</sub> from Table 19, depends on grade and p<sub>t</sub>
Three cases and the action in each
answer: Nominal shear stress τ<sub>v</sub> = V<sub>u</sub>/(b d): V<sub>u</sub> is the factored shear (N), b the width or web width (mm), d the effective depth (mm). It is an average stress used for design, not the true peak.

Design shear strength of concrete τ<sub>c</sub> (IS 456 Table 19): the shear stress the concrete carries without shear steel. It rises with the grade and with p<sub>t</sub> = 100 A<sub>st</sub>/(b d), counting only bars that continue at least d beyond the section, because more steel keeps cracks narrower and dowels stronger.
Maximum shear stress τ<sub>c,max</sub> (Table 20): the ceiling on τ<sub>v</sub> even with shear steel, 2.8, 3.1 and 3.5 N/mm² for M20, M25 and M30. It protects the inclined struts against crushing.

head: Case
Action
rows: design stirrups for V<sub>us</sub> = V<sub>u</sub> − τ<sub>c</sub> b d
enlarge b or d, or raise the grade

answer: Example: b = 300 mm, d = 550 mm, three 25 mm bars (p<sub>t</sub> = 0.89 %), M25, V<sub>u</sub> = 180 kN. τ<sub>v</sub> = 180,000/165,000 = 1.09 N/mm²; τ<sub>c</sub> = 0.57 + (0.89 − 0.75)/0.25 × 0.07 = 0.61 N/mm²; τ<sub>c,max</sub> = 3.1 N/mm². The middle case applies: V<sub>us</sub> = 180 − 0.61 × 165,000/1000 = 79.35 kN.

Critical section: where the support reaction compresses the end of the beam, load within d of the face travels straight to the support through a concrete strut and no full inclined crack can form there. IS 456 therefore takes the section at d from the face as critical and designs the region nearer the support for the same shear.
Check: τ<sub>c</sub> b d + V<sub>us</sub> = 100.65 + 79.35 = 180 kN = V<sub>u</sub>, and τ<sub>v</sub> = 1.09 < 3.1 N/mm², so the section size is acceptable.

bank.q: Explain what bond between steel and concrete is and where it comes from. Derive the development length and give the IS 456 design bond stresses.
answer: Bond is the shear stress along the surface of a bar that transfers force between the bar and the concrete, so that the two strain together.

Sources: adhesion of the cement paste (lost at very small slip); friction once the bar slides, helped by shrinkage gripping the bar; and mechanical bearing of the ribs of deformed bars on the concrete, the main source for modern TMT bars.

Flexural bond is needed wherever the bar force changes because the moment changes. Anchorage bond is needed at bar ends, where the whole force passes into the concrete. In the limit state method IS 456 checks anchorage through development length rather than local flexural bond stress.
Failure: pull-out (the bar shears the concrete between its ribs) when the concrete is well confined; splitting of the cover along the bar when the cover is thin or bars are crowded.

answer.text: Derivation. Bar force = bond force over the length L<sub>d</sub>:
answer.pre:
σ<sub>s</sub> × π φ²/4 = τ<sub>bd</sub> × π φ × L<sub>d</sub>
L<sub>d</sub> = φ σ<sub>s</sub>/(4 τ<sub>bd</sub>),   σ<sub>s</sub> = 0.87 f<sub>y</sub>

answer.text: IS 456 bond stresses for plain bars in tension, and the modified values:

answer: Bundled bars: increase L<sub>d</sub> by 10, 20 and 33 % for two, three and four bars in contact.
Example: 16 mm Fe415 deformed bar in M25. σ<sub>s</sub> = 361.05 N/mm²; L<sub>d</sub> = 16 × 361.05/(4 × 2.24) = 644.7 mm (40.3φ) in tension; in compression 16 × 361.05/(4 × 2.80) = 515.8 mm.
Check: bond force 2.24 × π × 16 × 644.7 = 72.6 kN equals the bar force 361.05 × 201.1 = 72.6 kN.

bank.q: State the IS 456 rules for lap splices in tension and in compression, and explain why laps are staggered.
outline: Flexural tension: greater of L<sub>d</sub> and 30φ
Direct tension: greater of 2 L<sub>d</sub> and 30φ
Smaller bar governs; no laps above 36 mm
answer: Flexural tension: lap = greater of L<sub>d</sub> and 30φ. Direct tension: greater of 2 L<sub>d</sub> and 30φ. The straight length of a lap is at least 15φ or 200 mm.

Increase the tension lap by 1.4 for a bar at the top of a section as cast with cover below 2φ, or at a corner with cover below 2φ, or where adjacent laps are closer than 75 mm or 6φ; by 2.0 if both apply.
Compression: lap = development length in compression, but not less than 24φ.
Bars of different diameters: base the lap on the smaller bar. Bars larger than 36 mm are not lapped; they are welded or coupled.

answer.text: Example, 16 mm Fe415 bars in M25:

answer: Staggering: a lap doubles the steel over a short length and relies on bond between two bars, so it is crowded and cracks first. If all bars lap at one section, that whole section is weak. Not more than half the bars are spliced at a section, laps count as staggered when their centres are at least 1.3 times the lap length apart (845 mm for a 650 mm lap), and laps are kept away from sections where the moment exceeds half the moment of resistance.
Check: 650 mm ≥ L<sub>d</sub> = 645 mm and ≥ 30φ = 480 mm, so the flexural lap satisfies both conditions.

bank.q: A simply supported beam 250 mm wide with effective depth 450 mm has a clear span of 5.0 m and a factored load of 75 kN/m. Concrete is M25, steel Fe415, and three 20 mm bars run into the supports. Design two-legged 8 mm vertical stirrups and give the spacing zones along the span.
outline: Shear at the face and at d
Zone change from the shear diagram
answer: Shear at the support face: V = 75 × 5.0/2 = 187.5 kN. At the critical section, 0.45 m from the face: V<sub>u</sub> = 187.5 − 75 × 0.45 = 153.75 kN.
τ<sub>v</sub> = 153.75 × 10³/(250 × 450) = 1.37 N/mm². τ<sub>c,max</sub> = 3.1 N/mm² for M25, so the section is adequate.

A<sub>st</sub> = 3 × 314.2 = 942.5 mm²; p<sub>t</sub> = 100 × 942.5/112,500 = 0.84 %. Table 19, M25: τ<sub>c</sub> = 0.57 + (0.84 − 0.75)/0.25 × 0.07 = 0.59 N/mm². τ<sub>v</sub> > τ<sub>c</sub>, so stirrups must be designed.

answer.text: Spacing of two-legged 8 mm Fe415 stirrups (A<sub>sv</sub> = 100.5 mm²):

answer: With the widest allowed spacing, 300 mm: 66.4 + 54.4 = 120.8 kN. The shear falls to 120.8 kN at x = (187.5 − 120.8)/75 = 0.89 m from the face, so run the 180 mm spacing to 1.0 m.
Check: at 1.0 m the shear is 187.5 − 75 = 112.5 kN < 120.8 kN, so the wider zone is safe; at midspan the shear is zero and the 300 mm stirrups are the code minimum.

bank.q: An edge beam 300 mm × 600 mm (d = 545 mm) carries M<sub>u</sub> = 160 kN·m, V<sub>u</sub> = 180 kN and T<sub>u</sub> = 40 kN·m at a section. Use M25, Fe415, nominal cover 30 mm and 12 mm closed stirrups. Design the longitudinal and transverse reinforcement.
outline: V<sub>e</sub>, τ<sub>ve</sub> and the τ<sub>c,max</sub> check
M<sub>t</sub>, M<sub>e1</sub> and whether M<sub>e2</sub> is needed
Stirrups from the torsion formula and the limits
answer: Equivalent shear: V<sub>e</sub> = 180 + 1.6 × 40/0.3 = 393.3 kN. τ<sub>ve</sub> = 393.3 × 10³/(300 × 545) = 2.41 N/mm² < τ<sub>c,max</sub> = 3.1 N/mm². Section adequate.
Equivalent moment: M<sub>t</sub> = 40 × (1 + 600/300)/1.7 = 70.59 kN·m. M<sub>t</sub> < M<sub>u</sub>, so no M<sub>e2</sub>. M<sub>e1</sub> = 160 + 70.59 = 230.59 kN·m.

M<sub>u,lim</sub> = 0.138 × 25 × 300 × 545² = 307.4 kN·m > 230.59, so singly reinforced. Solving 230.59 × 10⁶ = 0.87 × 415 A<sub>st</sub> × 545 (1 − 415 A<sub>st</sub>/(300 × 545 × 25)) gives A<sub>st</sub> = 1360 mm².
Provide three 25 mm bars (1473 mm²). x<sub>u</sub> = 0.87 × 415 × 1473/(0.36 × 25 × 300) = 196.9 mm < 0.48 × 545 = 261.6 mm; M<sub>R</sub> = 246.2 kN·m ≥ 230.59 kN·m. Top: two 12 mm corner bars.
p<sub>t</sub> = 100 × 1473/(300 × 545) = 0.90 %; τ<sub>c</sub> = 0.57 + (0.90 − 0.75)/0.25 × 0.07 = 0.61 N/mm² < τ<sub>ve</sub>, so torsion stirrups are designed.
Corner-bar centres: bottom 30 + 12 + 12.5 = 54.5 mm, top 30 + 12 + 6 = 48 mm from the faces; b<sub>1</sub> = 300 − 109 = 191 mm, d<sub>1</sub> = 600 − 54.5 − 48 = 497.5 mm.

answer.text: Two-legged 12 mm stirrups, A<sub>sv</sub> = 226.2 mm², 0.87 f<sub>y</sub> A<sub>sv</sub> = 81,668 N:

answer: Provide 12 mm closed stirrups at 140 mm with 135° hooks.
Side faces: D = 600 > 450 mm, so 0.1 % × 300 × 600 = 180 mm²: one 12 mm bar on each face at mid-depth.
Check: τ<sub>ve</sub> = 2.41 < 3.1 N/mm², M<sub>R</sub> = 246.2 ≥ 230.6 kN·m, and 140 mm is below 144.4, 151.6, 189, 228 and 300 mm.

bank.q: A beam 230 mm wide (d = 400 mm, M20, Fe415) rests on a 230 mm wall; two 16 mm bottom bars run into the support with 30 mm end cover, and the shear at the support is 100 kN. Check the anchorage and decide whether a 90° bend is needed.
answer: τ<sub>bd</sub> for M20 deformed bars in tension = 1.2 × 1.6 = 1.92 N/mm². L<sub>d</sub> = 16 × 361.05/(4 × 1.92) = 752.2 mm.
1.3 M<sub>1</sub>/V = 1.3 × 52.78 × 10⁶/(100 × 10³) = 686.1 mm (the reaction confines the bar ends, so 1.3 applies).
L<sub>0</sub> for straight bars = 230/2 − 30 = 85 mm. 1.3 M<sub>1</sub>/V + L<sub>0</sub> = 686.1 + 85 = 771.1 mm ≥ 752.2 mm: the diameter is acceptable.
Length into the support: L<sub>d</sub>/3 = 250.7 mm, but only 230 − 30 = 200 mm is available. Straight bars fail this rule.
With a 90° bend at the end, its anchorage value 8φ = 128 mm counts: 200 + 128 = 328 mm ≥ 250.7 mm. The bend also raises L<sub>0</sub> to 85 + 128 = 213 mm.
Conclusion: bend both bars up 90° at the far face of the wall (inside the cover). Check: 686.1 + 213 = 899.1 mm and 328 mm both exceed their requirements.

bank.q: At a section of a beam b = 300 mm, d = 500 mm, the stirrups must carry V<sub>us</sub> = 90 kN. Using two-legged 10 mm Fe415 stirrups, find the spacing and check the minimum shear reinforcement and maximum spacing.
answer: Maximum spacing: least of 0.75 × 500 = 375 mm and 300 mm, so 300 mm.
Adopt 300 mm: the code maximum governs, not strength.

bank.q: Prepare the reinforcement detailing of the edge beam of the combined bending, shear and torsion chapter (300 × 600 mm; four 20 mm bottom bars, two 12 mm top bars, one 12 mm side bar each face, 10 mm closed stirrups at 140 mm; 6 m clear span), showing the section, the elevation and the checks.
answer: Cover: moderate exposure, nominal cover 30 mm to the 10 mm stirrups, so 40 mm to the main bars; d = 600 − 30 − 10 − 10 = 550 mm.
Clear spacing of the bottom bars: (300 − 60 − 20 − 80)/3 = 46.7 mm, between the minimum 25 mm (20 mm aggregate + 5) and the maximum 180 mm (Fe415).
Stirrups: closed, 10 mm, 135° hooks with 6φ = 60 mm extensions bent round a corner bar, because torsion cracks spiral and can spall a 90° hook out of the cover.
Corner bars: a bar in every corner of the stirrup (two 20 mm at the bottom corners, two 12 mm at the top). Side faces: D > 450 mm, one 12 mm bar each face at mid-depth, gaps 254 and 250 mm ≤ 300 mm.

bank.q: IS 456 designs a beam for torsion through equivalent shear and equivalent moment rather than torsion theory. Explain why, and discuss where this simplification can mislead a designer.
outline: Cracked torsion is a space truss; the analysis is complex
Equivalent actions reuse shear and flexure tools
Where it misleads: compatibility torsion, M<sub>e2</sub> near supports, flanged and thin-walled sections, detailing
answer: Why. After cracking a beam in torsion behaves as a space truss: closed stirrups as hoops, corner bars as stringers and spiral concrete struts. An exact design needs the shear-flow area, strut angle and interaction with bending and shear. IS 456 replaces this with two familiar actions: V<sub>e</sub> = V<sub>u</sub> + 1.6 T<sub>u</sub>/b for the web and the stirrups, and M<sub>t</sub> = T<sub>u</sub> (1 + D/b)/1.7 added to M<sub>u</sub> for the longitudinal bars. The designer then uses the ordinary shear check and flexure tables (such as SP 16).

The factors 1.6 and 1.7 are calibrated against tests on solid rectangular beams, and the method keeps the key physics: torsion needs both transverse and longitudinal steel, and the web can crush (τ<sub>ve</sub> ≤ τ<sub>c,max</sub>).

answer.text: Illustration, edge beam 300 × 600 mm, d = 550 mm, M<sub>u</sub> = 150 kN·m, V<sub>u</sub> = 120 kN, T<sub>u</sub> = 30 kN·m:

answer: Where it can mislead (1): compatibility torsion. Applied blindly, it designs torsion that IS 456 allows to be neglected, or worse, a designer releases torsion that is actually equilibrium torsion (an edge beam carrying a canopy). The method does not classify the torsion; the designer must.

(2) Near supports M<sub>u</sub> is small. In the example, at M<sub>u</sub> = 30 kN·m, M<sub>t</sub> = 52.94 > M<sub>u</sub>, so M<sub>e2</sub> = 22.94 kN·m puts the top face in tension. A designer who checks only midspan, or stops the top bars as hangers, misses this.

(3) Flanged, hollow or thin-walled sections: the calibration is for solid rectangles. Using b of the web alone ignores the flanges' torsional resistance in some cases and overstates it in others; box girders need the thin-walled tube model.

(4) Detailing is not in the formulas: closed stirrups with 135° hooks, a bar in each corner, side bars beyond 450 mm depth, and anchorage of longitudinal bars at supports. A section that passes the numbers but has open stirrups will fail by spiral cracking.

Evaluation: the method is adequate and conservative for ordinary rectangular beams under equilibrium torsion, provided the designer classifies the torsion, checks M<sub>e2</sub> wherever M<sub>u</sub> is small and details a closed cage. Check from the illustration: 280 × 10³/(300 × 550) = 1.70 N/mm² < 3.1, so the section works.

bank.q: A contractor stops half of the bottom bars of a beam exactly where the bending moment diagram shows they are no longer needed. Analyse what can go wrong and state what IS 456 requires, with the beam of the curtailment worked example (6 m span, four 16 mm bars, d = 450 mm, M<sub>u</sub> = 110 kN·m).
outline: Theoretical cut-off from M<sub>R</sub> of the remaining bars
Shift of bar force by inclined cracks
Development length of the stopped and continuing bars
Shear condition at a cut-off in tension
answer: Theoretical cut-off: two 16 mm bars give M<sub>R</sub> = 62.1 kN·m (x<sub>u</sub> = 53.8 mm). With M(x) = 110 × 4x(6 − x)/36, M = 62.1 kN·m at x = 1.02 m from each support. The contractor stops the bars at 1.02 m.

What goes wrong (1): an inclined crack starting near 1.02 m carries the steel force towards the support; the tension at the crack is governed by the moment further along the crack, roughly d towards midspan. The remaining two bars are then overstressed just where they have been left alone.

(2) The stopped bars have no length beyond the point where they are needed to develop force; a crack at the bar end becomes a sudden step in stiffness and steel stress, and flexural cracks open wide there.

(3) At a cut-off in a tension zone the shear capacity is reduced; IS 456 allows the cut-off only if the shear there is at most two thirds of the capacity (or extra stirrups or double steel are provided).

answer.text: What IS 456 requires, worked for this beam:

answer: The continuing bars must also run at least L<sub>d</sub> = 645 mm beyond the theoretical cut-off (they run to the support and beyond, about 1.02 m plus anchorage), and at least one third of the bars must enter the support for L<sub>d</sub>/3 = 215 mm.
If the contractor's cut at 1.02 m stayed, the shear there would be 24.44 × (3 − 1.02) = 48.4 kN; the shear check would pass, but the extension rule would not, which is the main error.
Check: the bars from 0.57 to 5.43 m provide 4 bars wherever M > 62.1 kN·m (1.02 to 4.98 m) with 450 mm to spare at each end, so the rules are met.

bank.q: Discuss how the shear span to depth ratio, the concrete grade and the stirrup spacing change the shear behaviour and failure of a beam.
outline: Stirrups turn a brittle failure into a ductile one

head: a/d
Behaviour
Failure
rows: arch action, load goes straight to support
strut crushing or splitting, anchorage of tie
inclined crack forms, beam carries more load

answer: Example: a point load 1.2 m from the support with d = 400 mm gives a/d = 3.0, the diagonal tension range: the beam needs stirrups to avoid a sudden split.

Concrete grade: τ<sub>c</sub> rises with grade (at p<sub>t</sub> = 1.00 %, 0.62, 0.64 and 0.66 N/mm² for M20, M25, M30) and τ<sub>c,max</sub> rises more (2.8, 3.1, 3.5 N/mm²). A higher grade mainly protects against web crushing; it adds little to the concrete share.
Steel percentage: at M25, τ<sub>c</sub> goes from 0.36 at p<sub>t</sub> = 0.25 % to 0.64 at 1.00 %, so heavily reinforced beams carry more shear without stirrups.

Stirrups: before cracking they do little; after it they tie the crack, keep aggregate interlock and dowels working, and yield before the concrete fails, so the failure becomes gradual. Their contribution is V<sub>us</sub> = 0.87 f<sub>y</sub> A<sub>sv</sub> d/s<sub>v</sub>.

Spacing: close stirrups make sure every 45° crack crosses several of them; hence s<sub>v</sub> ≤ 0.75 d and 300 mm. In the 6 m beam with w<sub>u</sub> = 80 kN/m, stirrups at 200 mm carry 200.4 kN with the concrete, enough for 196 kN at d; at 300 mm only 167.2 kN, so the close zone runs to 1.0 m.
Too much shear steel does not help beyond τ<sub>c,max</sub>, because the struts crush first.
Check: τ<sub>v</sub> = 1.19 N/mm² in that beam is between τ<sub>c</sub> = 0.61 and τ<sub>c,max</sub> = 3.1 N/mm², so stirrups (not a bigger section) are the correct remedy.

bank.q: Evaluate how far detailing (cover, spacing, anchorage, laps and stirrup hooks) decides the real safety of a beam. Use the interaction of bond and shear in your answer.
outline: Calculated steel works only if it can develop its force
Anchorage at supports where shear is highest
answer: A design gives areas of steel; detailing decides whether each bar can actually reach 0.87 f<sub>y</sub>. Every rule exists because of a failure that the strength calculation does not see.

Cover: nominal cover (30 mm for moderate exposure, to the stirrups) protects against corrosion and fire, and resists splitting of the concrete along deformed bars. Thin cover means rust, spalling and a splitting bond failure at a lower load.

Spacing: the clear gap must be at least the bar size and aggregate + 5 mm so concrete can surround each bar (46.7 mm in the edge beam is fine), and at most 180 mm for Fe415 to control crack width. Crowded bars leave voids and lose bond.

Bond and shear interact at supports. Near a support the shear is largest and an inclined crack moves the bar force towards the support, so the bars need anchorage exactly where the moment is small. In the support example, two 20 mm bars needed L<sub>d</sub> = 806 mm ≤ 1.3 M<sub>1</sub>/V + L<sub>0</sub> = 964 mm; with 25 mm bars, L<sub>d</sub> = 1007 mm passed that check but the length into the support (L<sub>d</sub>/3 = 336 mm > 270 mm) failed without a bend.

Laps and cut-offs: a lap shorter than max(L<sub>d</sub>, 30φ) behaves like a short anchorage and pulls out; bunched laps create a weak section. A bar stopped at its theoretical cut-off is overstressed by the shift from inclined cracks; the extension d or 12φ (450 mm in the 6 m beam) covers this.

Hooks and stirrups: a stirrup is anchored only with 90° + 8φ, 135° + 6φ or 180° + 4φ. Under torsion or cyclic load the 135° hook keeps the hoop closed after the cover spalls. An open or poorly hooked stirrup carries none of the V<sub>us</sub> assumed in design.

answer.text: Summary of the numbers from the worked examples:

answer: Evaluation: detailing is part of design, not drafting. The strength checks are necessary but not sufficient; a beam with correct areas and poor detailing fails at a support, a lap or a hook before its calculated capacity. Check: every requirement in the table is met by the provided value, so the example beams are safe as detailed.

glossary.def: Distance from a point load to the nearer support, a; the ratio a/d decides the mode of shear failure.
A crack that starts vertical at the soffit and turns inclined towards the load where both moment and shear are large.
An inclined crack that opens first inside a thin web near the neutral axis, close to a support.
Shear passed across a narrow crack by friction between its rough faces.
Shear carried by the main bars bending locally where they cross a crack.
Model of a cracked beam as a truss with concrete struts, stirrup ties and the main steel and compression zone as chords.
Crushing of the inclined concrete struts in a thin web under heavy shear, prevented by the τ<sub>c,max</sub> limit.
A closed or open link round the main bars that carries shear and holds the cage together.
A main bar bent up near a support to act as inclined shear reinforcement; it may carry at most half of the shear steel's share.
Torque the member must carry to keep the structure in equilibrium; it must be designed for.
Torque that arises only because members are monolithic; IS 456 lets it be neglected if torsional stiffness is ignored in the analysis.
Model of a cracked beam in torsion: closed stirrups as hoops, corner bars as stringers, spiral concrete struts.
Failure of a beam under bending and torsion along a spiral crack on three faces with crushing on the fourth.
Longitudinal bars on the side faces of deep webs, 0.1 % of the web area, at 300 mm or less.
Transfer of force between a bar and the concrete by adhesion, friction and the bearing of ribs.
Bond needed where the bar force changes along the beam because the moment changes.
Bond needed at a bar end, where the whole bar force passes into the concrete.
Bond failure in which the wedging of the ribs splits the cover along the bar.
A U-type bar end with an anchorage value of 16φ; a 90° bend is worth 8φ.
Overlap of two bars that passes force from one to the other through the concrete.
A threaded or swaged sleeve that joins two bars end to end, used for large bars and crowded sections.
Where the moment falls to the moment of resistance of the bars that continue.
Design cover to all steel including links, set by the exposure class.
Distance from the compression face to the centroid of the tension steel, d.
List of every bar with its mark, diameter, shape, number, cutting length and weight.
